This summer has been extremely hot.

Television and the Internet have repeatedly reported that this is heat not seen for decades.

Many people have also died from heatstroke.

In addition, apparently, the glaciers in the Arctic are melting considerably.

Rainfall patterns are also gradually changing significantly compared with the past.

Regardless of the forecast, torrential rain is falling in large amounts, causing extensive loss of life and property.

At this rate, wherever or whenever a larger disaster occurs, it would not be surprising… (the rest omitted)

Writing is originally something used for writing and reading, so surely no one finds this strange.

As mechanical civilization has developed, we write less and less.

default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t11-p1.vietnamese:
Below is an email from Kwon Young-soo to his acquaintance in Japan, Oyabu Kazuto.

Recipient: yumenokuni@darakwon.co.jp

Subject: How have you been?

Dear Mr. Oyabu,
How have you been recently?

The publication celebration in Tokyo the other day was truly wonderful.

I was deeply moved that so many people came to attend because of the humble little book I wrote myself.

In particular, I never even dreamed that the president of your company and his wife would personally attend.

I also took a few photographs, so I will send them to you as soon as they are ready.

If you ever have a chance to come to Seoul, please be sure to contact me. I very much look forward to welcoming you.

Take care, and I wish you continued good health.

default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t12-p1.vietnamese:
The term “doing-one-thing-while-doing-another group” appeared decades ago and means “a group of people who do one thing while doing another.”

Actually, when I was a student, I was much more in the habit of doing one thing while doing another than most people.

However, now that I am over fifty and look back on the past, I believe that this cannot be called a good thing at all.

Handling two tasks at the same time is merely an ideal; in reality, efficiency is very poor.

Driving while using a smartphone is not just ineffective—it is extremely dangerous.

(Note) 人一倍: far more than the average person.

default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t13-p1.vietnamese:
The loanword “risutora” (restructuring) began to be used quite some time ago, but I do not know its exact original meaning in English.

I merely assume that it means “cutting staff” in order to rebuild a business or company.

The reason I “assume” this is not that there are no dictionaries, nor that I am reluctant to look it up.

It is simply that whenever I read or hear the word, I do not get a positive feeling from it, so I have kept leaving it unexplained without looking it up.

Another reason is that whenever I encounter the word on online news portals or in television news reports, its meaning fits exactly with my assumption when I consider the surrounding context.

If my assumption is correct, the question is “why” this word is used so frequently.

Compared with not knowing the exact spelling and original meaning of the word, that question concerns me much more.

default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t14-p1.vietnamese:
Dear Ishikawa,

How have you been? This is Morita, your class representative during our second year of high school.

It has already been 22 years since we graduated from high school, hasn't it? Do you remember the promise that the 22 classmates from Class 2-2 would meet at 2 p.m. on February 22, 2019, in the grounds of our old school?

After that, some people were reachable and others were not, but I heard that you recently returned from the United States. I heard that you had been there for 15 years. I got your story and email address from Nagashima, whom I occasionally see.

Mr. Tanaka, who was our homeroom teacher back then, reached the mandatory retirement age the year before last and is now living in his hometown while farming.

Some of our classmates have had smooth and successful lives, while others have not, but I think the most important thing is that everyone is healthy. When we meet next time, I think stories such as the "ghost incident" that occurred during our hands-on trip back then will take us back to those nostalgic days.

Of course you will be attending, but before then, please send me a few words about how you have been recently.

default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t15-p1.vietnamese:
Dear Mr./Ms. Ando,

It has been very hot every day lately. I hope you are doing well.

The first semester is almost over, but I still feel that I have not completely adjusted to life here.

Indeed, studying and teaching are quite different.

It is very difficult to help students understand Japanese grammar and nuances accurately.

Nevertheless, spending time with the students every day is enjoyable.

I sometimes think back to the six years I spent studying abroad in Japan, and when I have free time, I often look through my old photographs.

By the way, there will be an academic seminar in Tokyo on July 27 (Wednesday), but I am probably unable to attend on the 27th because I will be busy grading final exams.

At present, I plan to arrive at Narita around noon on the 28th and may be able to reach the venue in Kudanshita at around 4:00 p.m.

Could you please collect the thesis materials distributed on the first day for me as well?

As for the business hotel, could you please confirm that it has been properly booked for two nights?

Fortunately, my presentation is scheduled for the second and final day of the seminar, so I will definitely be able to make it in time.

The topic of this seminar, 「Japanese Language Customs as Reflected in れる・られる」, is extremely interesting.

I intended to write an email, but my computer broke down, so please excuse me for sending this by fax.

I look forward to seeing you the day after tomorrow.

default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t16-p1.vietnamese:
Kyoko Tanimura is looking for a new room.

Since she does not have much money, she is first considering finding a very inexpensive room.

However, as a track-and-field athlete, it would be inconvenient not to have a bathtub.

She does not particularly care about the distance to the station or how bright the room is.

Which room best suits Kyoko Tanimura's requirements?

Kyoko Tanimura's friend Midori has invited her to share a room, so she is considering that option.

Since two people would be living together, the room must have two rooms.

In addition, her friend has a cat and often returns late from her part-time job, so the closer the room is to the station, the better.

Naturally, the cheaper the rent, the better. Which room meets these requirements?

default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t17-p1.vietnamese:
Factory A’s No-Smoking Rules

A manufacturer of automobile components recently introduced new rules at Factory A to reduce the number of smokers.

The new rules are as follows:

1) Smoking is permitted only at designated locations and during designated times (see the separate chart for the locations and times. Anyone who does not comply will receive 10 penalty points for each violation).

2) If a person’s penalty points exceed 30 points in a single month, they must clean the restrooms for one week.

3) Anyone who successfully refrains from smoking for an entire month will receive one paid day off.

(Note) このほど: recently

default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t18-p1.vietnamese:
I think that although the arrival of the Internet has made many things more convenient, there are also quite a few cases in which that is not necessarily true.

For example, when buying something, it is often difficult to know how much to trust reviews about it.

Recently, I once took the review "This book is very good" at face value and spent a large amount of money to buy the book, but I ended up disliking it so much that I was extremely disappointed.

I realized deeply that relying too heavily on the Internet is also something we need to consider carefully.

default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t19-p1.vietnamese:
The so-called “distance-shortening technique” in old movies literally means a technique for shrinking a long distance so that one can travel across it in an instant.

Of course, physically speaking, that is probably impossible.

However, aren't we actually using that very “distance-shortening technique” to live our lives today?

When I was in high school and exchanged letters with an American girl, the fastest a letter ever took was a full month for one round trip. An email, however, arrives in just a few seconds.

The survey showed that having too much work is not good, but having too little work—or no work at all—is not good either.

default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t21-p1.vietnamese:
I spent a long period working in Europe.

After graduating from university at the age of 24, I joined a company. Five years later, I began working at the Paris branch, and from then until I returned to Japan this year, I traveled throughout Europe for about 14 years.

I worked in five cities in three countries: starting in Paris, then moving to Marseille and Lyon, followed by Hamburg in neighboring Germany, and finally London.

As a result, my children speak French, German, and English fairly well, but their Japanese—the most essential language—is very poor.

When I returned to Japan at the age of 43, I began to worry about my children's future.

Although they are Japanese, they knew little about both the Japanese language and Japanese culture.

I still have many doubts and concerns about what Japan ultimately means to these children and whether it is truly their homeland.

I worried about everything: whether they would be bullied at school, and whether they would be able to live well and fit in later.

While everyone else was urging children to learn English, my family had to hire tutors to teach our children their mother tongue—it was a strange period of our lives.

Mice are of course animals, but I have never heard anyone say that they like mice.

In other words, this means that mice are disliked, apparently because, besides being “dirty” and “disgusting,” they can also transmit infectious diseases.

Furthermore, they eat the grain that people work hard to grow and harvest, so it can be said that they are disliked even more for that reason.

However, if we were told that it is precisely thanks to mice that our lives have become more hygienic and that we suffer from fewer illnesses, everyone would surely be surprised.

Although this way of putting it is paradoxical, it is thanks to mice, whose DNA is said to be very similar to that of humans, that we have been able to conduct many experiments.

In particular, thanks to laboratory mice, humans have been able to research and develop many different medicines.

default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t23-p1.vietnamese:
Several decades have passed since the disease called AIDS was discovered.

At first, everyone was afraid, and people took precautions to protect their own safety.

Of course, it is still a disease that requires caution now and in the future, but perhaps because of my own impression, it seems that people no longer urge others to take precautions as loudly as they once did.

Is it because sufficient knowledge about the seriousness of the disease has already spread?

Or has people's sense of concern faded because they have heard about it too many times?

A new strain of influenza once caused a major epidemic and stirred up public opinion, but this too seems to be creating a similar atmosphere.

Human beings are perhaps essentially 「very forgetful」 creatures.

There is an idiom, 「repaying a favor with resentment」. This means forgetting another person's help and kindness—that is, the favor received—and repaying it with resentment (an evil act or ill consequence).

This expression is usually used to suggest that someone who repays another person's kindness or help with evil means is a bad person, but I do not interpret it that way.

Instead, I see such people as individuals who are very prone to forget things that happened in the past.

When we analyze the kanji 「borrow」 (借), we see that it is made up of 「person (人) + long ago (昔)」.

The kanji 「long ago」 (昔) carries the meaning 「a very long time has passed」. In summary, this character is said to mean 「when a person borrows something from someone else, they let a very long time pass before returning it」.

There are many kanji that make us exclaim 「So that's how it is!」, and this is one of them.

Modern society currently faces all kinds of problems.

Bullying is one of them; it occurs not only in schools but has also spread to companies.

I think bullying has many causes, but one scholar argues that "human loneliness" is the cause.

Loneliness is harmful both to oneself and to others.

It seems that thoughtful measures are needed to prevent people from becoming isolated and from isolating others.

default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t28-p1.vietnamese:

default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t29-p1.vietnamese:
Everyone has a clock.

Normally, every household surely has at least one wall clock.

The mobile-phone ownership rate has also exceeded 100%. Apparently, this is because quite a few people use two or more phones.

Naturally, those phones have clocks built in.

Rice cookers, microwave ovens, driver's seats, and computer screens all have clocks as well. We are living in a world overflowing with clocks.

Because my work often takes me overseas, I judge whether a country is a pleasant place to live by the number of large clocks on its streets.

In my case, I wear a wristwatch, and there are clocks on both my camera and my phone, but when I am in a hurry, I do not even have time to look at them.

That is an exaggeration, but before I have time to put down my bag and check the time, I can often spot a large clock simply by looking around.

I like countries that are this convenient because I believe it shows thoughtful consideration for their citizens.

The following email was sent by Ohara Kazuyuki to his Korean friend, Park Myung-jin.

Recipient: yumenokuni@kokoro.co.jp

Subject: I arrived safely!

How are you, Park?

Thank you very much for all your help while I was visiting Korea.

Even though you were busy, you took me to see many places, and I am extremely grateful.

It had been a long time since I had seen Seoul’s night view, and it was beautiful. The galbi was also delicious.

I arrived safely in Tokyo on Saturday evening.

I will return to work tomorrow.

You are coming to Tokyo on a business trip next month, right?

When you do, please stay at my house.

Take care and stay healthy.

default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t30-p1.vietnamese:
Nowadays, Japan faces a social issue called a “declining birthrate” (fewer children).

Literally, this means that the number of children being born is gradually decreasing.

Nevertheless, although only slightly, the total population continues to increase.

A “declining birthrate” and an “increasing total population” may seem contradictory at first glance, but in reality, both are largely true.

The reason for this contradiction is that although the number of children being born is indeed decreasing, average life expectancy continues to grow.

Of course, if the situation of having fewer children continues indefinitely, the total population will eventually have no choice but to decline as well.

This is because, with current medical advances, increases in average life expectancy cannot continue forever.

More than that issue, what I want to discuss here is the weakening of production caused by having fewer children, as well as the increasing social burden on the elderly that results from it.

In fact, Japan has now stopped experiencing total population growth and is becoming a country with a declining population.

The waves of population aging and the declining birthrate are growing stronger, and it is difficult to say that the future looks bright.

default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t31-p1.outline.3.label: The roles of kanji and katakana
default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t31-p1.outline.3.note: Kanji compensates for the limited number of sounds and the many homophones in Japanese, while katakana distinguishes foreign-derived words; kanji is a highly valuable writing system.
default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t31-p1.vietnamese:
Some people claim that “Japanese has very few speech sounds,” but since it is impossible to investigate every language, it is difficult to say how valid this claim really is.

However, if Japanese is compared with the major international languages, the claim is not entirely unreasonable; it is partly true.

Of course, the so-called number of speech sounds is merely a comparison made when learning a foreign language. For Japanese people who use Japanese every day, it has nothing to do with their lives because they do not feel any inconvenience.

Changing the subject slightly, I think the reason that “characteristics of the Japanese language” and “the Japanese people” often become topics of discussion is that Japan stands out despite being a small Asian country, especially when viewed from countries with large territories. In addition to household electronics and automobiles, which are naturally well known, many Japanese words have entered English, and Japan is also a base for transmitting information originating in Japan.

Another characteristic of Japanese that is often discussed is “homophones with different meanings.” This concerns native Japanese words, not the many homophones commonly found among names written in kanji.

For example, when we say “hashi,” the word may refer to a “bridge” (橋), “chopsticks” (箸), or an “edge” (端), and it is very difficult to distinguish them when written in hiragana. Words such as “kaeru” are even more difficult because they can mean “to return” (帰る), “to change” (変える), “to return something” (返る), “to substitute” (代える), or “frog” (蛙).

Of course, when we converse, the overall context is available, so confusion about meaning hardly ever occurs.

Leaving theories aside, characteristics of Japanese such as “having few speech sounds and many homophones with different meanings” have been greatly compensated for by the introduction of kanji, which makes meanings easier to understand when written.

Moreover, katakana makes it easier to distinguish native Japanese words from foreign-derived words. In this sense, I think it is fair to say that kanji is an extremely valuable writing system.

Recently, a major disaster occurred when an airplane carrying up to 150 people crashed, reportedly because of a single damaged bolt.

default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t36-p1.vietnamese:
In our daily lives, we maintain relationships by talking and interacting with others.

It could be said that the main purpose of ordinary conversation is for other people to understand us.

default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t37-p1.vietnamese:
I believe that proverbs are wisdom created by the history of each country and people.

There are many proverbs from my own country that I like, but Japanese proverbs also include quite a few wonderful ones.

The proverb I would most like to mention is “Short temper, great loss” (短気は損気).

It means that “a short-tempered person is likely to suffer losses,” and conveys the lesson “do not rush to conclusions.”

For example, if you encounter something difficult to understand or accept at work and immediately submit your resignation, it is very likely that you will end up making the wrong decision. That is an example of “Short temper, great loss.”

There is also a similar proverb: “Silence is golden” (言わぬが花 - Not saying it is a flower).

This proverb means “do not rush to state a conclusion; remain silent,” advising us not to speak or act carelessly.

I came to like these proverbs because, in my own life so far, I have experienced quite a few situations that fit them.

I think we really should follow the wisdom of our predecessors. Although it may be somewhat cautious and passive, I feel that doing so is safer in many situations.

default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t38-p1.outline.0.label: Raising the question of life’s purpose
default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t38-p1.outline.0.note: The author opens with a thought-provoking question about each person’s purpose in life and comments on the different reactions people have when faced with it.
default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t38-p1.outline.1.label: A survey and student feedback
default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t38-p1.outline.1.note: The author had students write English essays about happiness and noted that most felt unhappy without knowing why. This provides the basis for question 1 about the occupation of an English teacher.
default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t38-p1.outline.2.label: The author's opinion and advice
default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t38-p1.outline.2.note: The author shares a perspective for making lessons more meaningful: people fail to realize that they are happy, either because they are too greedy or because they do not make enough effort (based on sentences 2 and 3).
default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t38-p1.outline.3.label: Vocabulary notes in the passage
default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t38-p1.outline.3.note: Explains the words marked in the passage: 番 (turn), 台詞 (line or spoken words), and 付け加える (add).
default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t38-p1.vietnamese:
If you were asked what you live for, how would you answer?

Some people would surely be able to answer immediately, while others would not.

I once gave this topic to the students I teach and asked them to write an essay in English.

The most common answer was “to become happy.”

Then, when I asked a similar question, “Are you happy now?”, the most common answer was “No, I do not feel happy.”

The following week, when I asked, “What do you think is the reason or cause that you do not feel happy?”, most people answered, “I am not really sure.”

Next, it was my turn. If I merely said, “I see,” it would not be very interesting as a lesson, would it?

My main explanation was: “Perhaps you think that way because you are happy but do not realize it?”

In addition, I added things such as being too greedy and lacking effort.

（Note 1）番 (turn): The order or sequence in which something is done

（Note 2）台詞 (line/remark): A reply or explanation

（Note 3）付け加える: To add or supplement

default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t39-p1.outline.0.label: The convenience of the Internet in daily life
default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t39-p1.outline.0.note: The Internet makes life more convenient by providing global news at home, music, reference materials, and video communication.
default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t39-p1.outline.1.label: The computer age and the risk of being disadvantaged by technological illiteracy.
default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t39-p1.outline.1.note: Nowadays, not knowing how to use a computer puts people at a disadvantage, as computers increasingly offer convenient printing and photo-editing functions.
default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t39-p1.outline.2.label: Anxieties and dangers arising from the Internet and computers
default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t39-p1.outline.2.note: The dark sides and dangers: fraudulent fake websites, inaccurate and unreliable materials, and the risk of hackers breaking into and damaging data.
default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t39-p1.outline.3.label: The drawbacks and fatigue brought by technology
default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t39-p1.outline.3.note: Learning security procedures is difficult, and data may be lost because of input errors, causing emotional distress; technology is convenient but can also make people more exhausted.
default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t39-p1.vietnamese:
Thanks to the Internet, we can now enjoy an extremely convenient life.

First of all, right from home, we can keep up not only with events in our own country but also with developments around the world.

We can listen to our favorite music and look up many different kinds of materials.

Video communication, which allows us to see the other person, is also available and is more convenient than email.

Moreover, if illiteracy was once a major problem, today computer illiteracy is the problem.

This is truly an age in which people who are not technologically literate are disadvantaged.

Computers gain new capabilities every day, and it is now entirely possible to print photographs ourselves.

In my case, I can freely edit photographs taken with either a digital camera or a smartphone and complete the finished product in my own room.

However, recently I have begun to feel somewhat uneasy about the Internet and computers—things I had assumed were entirely beneficial.

The "It's me, it's me" scam was originally a telephone-based financial scam, but recently fake websites have also appeared, causing financial crimes to grow increasingly large in scale.

Furthermore, I hear that a great deal of material posted by unidentified people cannot be trusted.

If information is false, it would be better not to have it at all.

In addition, cyberattacks, in which someone enters another person's computer to steal or destroy files, are frightening.

Learning how to use computers safely is also a burdensome task. Besides, there have been times when a data-entry error caused documents I had spent months carefully creating to disappear, leaving me so discouraged that I lost the will to live.

The Internet and computers are supposed to make life more convenient, yet instead they are making us even more exhausted.

default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t4-p1.outline.1.note: Pointing out that even people with illnesses can live long if their conditions are properly managed.

default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t4-p1.vietnamese:
"Longevity without illness" means living a long life without suffering from any illness.

There is no one who does not wish to live a long life.

However, even if someone has an illness, managing it well can allow that person to live as long as they wish.

Conversely, there are also occasional cases in which someone who has been very healthy suddenly becomes ill and collapses.

There have been several people like that around me, which surprised me.

Since longevity without illness is rare in reality, it seems that we need to pay close attention to managing illness skillfully.

default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t5-p1.outline.0.label: The emergence and versatility of smartphones
default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t5-p1.outline.0.note: The smartphone has made countless previously impossible things possible through its many functions, making it difficult for users to stop once they begin using it.
default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t5-p1.outline.1.label: The strong addictiveness of smartphones
default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t5-p1.outline.1.note: The author compares smartphones with cigarettes: both are highly addictive. If people forget their wallet, they may not go back for it, but if they forget their smartphone, they return for it even when they are already late for work.
default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t5-p1.outline.2.label: Another perspective: smartphones as essential work tools.
default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t5-p1.outline.2.note: Points out another fundamental reason: without a smartphone, it is impossible to answer calls from customers or business partners or remember numbers well enough to call them, making work impossible. The fear of being unable to work is even greater than the fear of addiction.
default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t5-p1.outline.3.label: Conclusion: smartphones are indispensable in daily life
default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t5-p1.outline.3.note: With its durability and expanding range of functions, the smartphone has become indispensable in everyday life.
default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t5-p1.vietnamese:
Thanks to the advent of smartphones, things that were previously unimaginable have become possible.

Not only the Internet but also countless functions such as a camera and voice recorder are built in; once you start using one, it is almost impossible to stop.

Apparently, some people even say, “If you try hard, you can quit smoking, but it is absolutely impossible to stop using a smartphone.”

To be honest, although people say that cigarettes are not easy to quit either, there is no doubt that smartphones are so addictive that it is difficult to describe.

If you leave your wallet at home when you go out, you will not go back for it as long as you have money for transportation. With a smartphone, however, people often go back home to get it even if it makes them late for work.

Rather than viewing this simply as smartphone addiction, it can also be considered from a slightly different perspective.

If you cannot hear an incoming call from a business partner or customer, you cannot do your job.

Even though you cannot remember any of the phone numbers stored in your phone, you cannot make outgoing calls either.

What is more frightening than addiction itself is being unable to work.

From models that are hard to damage even if dropped, to models with enhanced water resistance, and even flexible models that can be folded and put in a pocket, smartphones have become indispensable in our daily lives.

（Note）強化された：became stronger, was enhanced.

default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t6-p1.vietnamese:
Recently, it has become increasingly common to see young people with dyed hair.

According to the results of a questionnaire survey conducted by the Youth Federation, 40% of the 500 respondents (200 people) had dyed their hair at some point.

Among those who had never dyed their hair, 10% answered, "I want to try it someday," showing that about half of the respondents belong to the "brown-hair camp."

On the other hand, 30%—150 people—answered, "I have absolutely no intention of dyeing my hair."

When asked why they felt that way, 100 people said, "Because it looks improper or unattractive," and 50 said, "Because it costs money."

When those who had answered "because it costs money" were asked, "If you had the money, would you want to try dyeing your hair?" every one of them answered, "Yes," and the results showed that the brown-hair camp ultimately accounted for 60%.

However, another survey found that most corporate recruiters have a negative view of brown hair, so people may want to take this into consideration before applying for jobs.

default.p.2nd_dokkai_n3-t7-p1.vietnamese:
These days, hardly anyone is probably unfamiliar with “insurance.”

It can be described as “something that protects people who fall into difficult circumstances.”

In life, alongside happy events such as having a child, passing an exam, joining a company, getting married, opening a store, or succeeding, there are also unhappy events such as death, failing an exam, mandatory retirement, divorce, closing a store, or failure.

If the former are called positive events, the latter can be called negative events. In other words, the former may be called good fortune, while the latter may be called misfortune.

Of course, some events in the latter group cannot be called misfortunes. Events such as dying or retiring at the mandatory age cannot be prevented through human effort.

However, if either of those two examples occurs because of an unexpected accident or because someone is unwillingly forced into it, it is classified as a misfortune.

“Insurance” has the function of collecting contributions in advance from everyone in order to support people who encounter such misfortunes.

In other words, “insurance” is the act of collecting money in advance in preparation for the assumption that, at some time and somewhere, someone will experience such an event.

In life, there are things everyone hopes for and things no one wants to happen. It can be said that we created “insurance” for precisely those reasons.

default.q.2nd_dokkai_n3-t1-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (b) 北極の氷河が解けて暑くなった。
The passage uses only the conjunction 「また」to add the phenomenon of melting Arctic ice; it does not claim that this phenomenon caused the hot weather.
default.q.2nd_dokkai_n3-t1-q1.explanation: The passage contains the quoted sentence: 「また、北極の氷河もだいぶ解けているという。」which means: “Furthermore, I hear that the glaciers in the Arctic have also melted considerably.” Here, the conjunction 「また」at the beginning adds new information independently, with the sense of “moreover” or “in addition.” It is used with the reporting pattern 「plain form + という」(“I hear that...”), not to express a cause-and-effect relationship. Choice (b), on the other hand, uses the connective form 「～て」(解けて) to express causation, giving the meaning: “The Arctic glaciers melted, causing the weather to become hot.” A common reading-comprehension trap is scanning only for keywords, so distinguish parallel information linked by 「また」from an incorrectly assigned causal relationship in an answer choice.
default.q.2nd_dokkai_n3-t1-q1.why.0: ✗ (a) This content matches the sentence 「熱中症で死んだ人も多数出た。」 in the passage, so it is not the choice with an incorrect connection.
default.q.2nd_dokkai_n3-t1-q1.why.1: ✓ (b) Correct because the passage does not mention a causal relationship in which melting ice causes the weather to become hotter; it simply uses the conjunction「また」to list another phenomenon.
default.q.2nd_dokkai_n3-t1-q1.why.2: ✗ (c) The passage clearly states that the phrase appeared decades ago: 「『地球温暖化』…という言葉が生まれたのも、もう何十年も前のことなのに」.
default.q.2nd_dokkai_n3-t1-q1.why.3: ✗ (d) Incorrect because the information about human efforts does not fully match the sentence 「まだまだそれを解決するための人間の努力は足りない。」 in the passage.
default.q.2nd_dokkai_n3-t10-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) 機械が発達して、書く代わりに機械に入力する機会が増えてきたから
The passage clearly states that we write fewer characters because machines have developed, causing people to switch from handwriting to entering text on electronic devices.
default.q.2nd_dokkai_n3-t10-q1.explanation: The direct evidence is: 「機械文明の発達により、私たちは、字をあまり書かなくなっています。字は書くよりも、打つものだと認識している人も多いようです。」 (“Due to the development of mechanical civilization, we have begun writing by hand less often. It seems that many people think of writing as something to type rather than something to write by hand.”) The author uses the comparison pattern 「V-る＋よりも」 (“rather than doing V”) in 「書くよりも、打つ」. This has a meaning similar to the grammar pattern 「V-る＋代わりに」, which replaces one action with another in a particular situation, as reflected in (c). In addition, the formal written expression 「N＋により」 gives an objective cause, corresponding to 「機械が発達して」. Test takers may confuse this with (a) because 「読む」 appears at the beginning of the passage. However, the cause-and-effect relationship shows that the passage discusses a change in how characters are produced—from handwriting to typing—not the importance of reading.
default.q.2nd_dokkai_n3-t10-q1.why.0: ✗ (a) The passage does not mention that reading characters has become more important than writing them; it only discusses the decline of handwriting.
default.q.2nd_dokkai_n3-t10-q1.why.1: ✗ (b) The passage does not mention that people are required to learn or practice skills for operating machinery.
default.q.2nd_dokkai_n3-t10-q1.why.2: ✓ (c) Correct because the passage states that the development of machine-based civilization has led many people to regard characters as something to type rather than write. In other words, opportunities to enter text into machines have increasingly replaced handwriting.
default.q.2nd_dokkai_n3-t10-q1.why.3: ✗ (d) The detail about working people is only intended to show that they rarely write by hand; the author does not say that they lack free time to write.
default.q.2nd_dokkai_n3-t11-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (d) 出版社の社長と奥様が一緒にパーティーに参加したこと
The author uses the adverb 「特に」 together with the idiom 「夢にも思いませんでした」 to emphasize that the publishing company president and his wife personally attending the party was the most unexpected and delightful event.
default.q.2nd_dokkai_n3-t11-q1.explanation: The author expresses the strongest emotion in the sentence: 「特に御社の社長ご夫妻がお見えになるとは、夢にも思いませんでした。」(I never dreamed that the president of your company and his wife would personally attend.) The key grammar pattern is 「plain form + とは夢にも思わなかった」, expressing extreme surprise at an unexpected event far beyond one’s expectations. It is combined with the honorific expression 「お見えになる」, the respectful form of 「来る」, showing deep respect and gratitude. In addition, the adverb 「特に」(especially) at the beginning singles out this event and raises its emotional importance above all the others at the party. Choice (a) may be tempting because of 「感動いたしました」in the preceding sentence, but for reading-comprehension questions such as 「何が一番…」, pay attention to focusing expressions such as 「特に」.
default.q.2nd_dokkai_n3-t11-q1.why.0: ✗ (a) Although the large turnout moved the author, it was not the most special or greatest source of joy.
default.q.2nd_dokkai_n3-t11-q1.why.1: ✗ (b) The book-launch celebration is merely the general setting of the event, not what made the author happiest.
default.q.2nd_dokkai_n3-t11-q1.why.2: ✗ (c) The letter only mentions that the writer took a few photographs and will send them later; it does not mention whether the photographs are interesting.
default.q.2nd_dokkai_n3-t11-q1.why.3: ✓ (d) The author emphasizes that the director and the director’s spouse attended together with the adverb 「特に」 and the structure 「夢にも思いませんでした」, expressing the greatest joy and honor.
default.q.2nd_dokkai_n3-t12-q1.verdict:

Here, 「叫ぶ」(to call out, urge, or warn) is used in the negative passive form 「叫ばれていない」 to objectively express that the community no longer raises warnings about this disease as actively as it did when it first appeared. The phrase 「あまり言われなくなった」(is no longer talked about as much) in choice (b) is the most accurate paraphrase of the reduced level of warnings expressed by 「叫ばれていない」. Remember that the comparison point before 「ほど」 represents the higher degree: people warned more in the past than they do now. This immediately rules out traps suggesting no change, such as (a)「昔も今も」, or an increased level, such as (c)「今でも話題」 and (d)「昔以上に」.

The complete meaning is: “Of course, among the latter examples, there are some that cannot be called that. Death and mandatory retirement, for example, are not things that can be prevented through human effort. However, if the two examples just mentioned occur because of an unexpected accident or because someone is forced into them against their wishes, they would be considered misfortune.” The key distinction is inevitability: (a) 不合格, (b) 離婚, and (d) 失敗 are purely negative events that people can generally take steps to avoid, whereas 「定年退職」 is simply an age-related social milestone. default.q.2nd_dokkai_n3-t9-q1.explanation: The key N3 grammar points are the superlative-like comparison「Noun + より...はない」, which follows a noun and emphatically states that nothing surpasses it, and「AよりもB」, which places greater emphasis on B than on A. These guide the reader from a traditional belief to the author’s new insight. The opening sentence is「犬より忠誠心の強い動物はない。」(“There is no animal more loyal than a dog”), while the conclusion is「犬は忠誠心よりも、ある意味では頭がいい動物である。」(“In a sense, dogs are intelligent animals rather than merely loyal ones”). The author uses the news story about a dog walking 500 km home to demonstrate its superior intelligence, not to praise its loyalty. Therefore, (c) is least related to the passage: it misinterprets the purpose of the news report and adds「さらに話題になった」(it became an even bigger topic of discussion), although the passage never mentions public reaction. Learners may confuse this with (d) because it repeats a similar comparative expression from the conclusion. However, read「関係が薄い」(least related) carefully and beware of choices that reuse familiar keywords while adding intensifying adverbs such as「さらに」to create unsupported information.
